modules.title: Programming Foundations and Complexity
modules.summary: How a Java program runs, how memory is laid out, and how Big-O describes growth.
modules.overview: Every data structure in this course is built from a few Java building blocks: primitive variables, references, arrays, loops and methods. This module makes those exact, then introduces the one tool used to compare every algorithm that follows: counting how the number of steps grows as the input grows.
objectives: Explain the difference between a primitive value and a reference in Java.
Trace a loop by hand and count how many times its body runs.
Give the Big-O time and space of a short program and justify it.
Recognise O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n log n) and O(n²) from the shape of the code.

concepts.title: Primitives and references
concepts.body: An int, long, double, char or boolean variable holds its value directly. Everything else — arrays, Strings, objects — is held by reference: the variable stores where the object lives on the heap. Assigning a reference copies the address, not the object, so two variables can point at the same array.

concepts.title: The call stack
concepts.body: Each method call gets a stack frame holding its parameters and local variables. When the method returns, the frame is removed. Recursion later in the course is just many frames of the same method on this stack.

concepts.title: Counting steps, not seconds
concepts.body: Seconds depend on the machine. Instead, count basic steps — a comparison, an assignment, an array read — as a function of the input size n, then keep only the fastest-growing term. 3n + 5 steps is O(n); n²/2 + n is O(n²).

concepts.title: Space complexity
concepts.body: Count the extra memory the algorithm creates, not the input itself. A few int variables is O(1). A new array the size of the input is O(n). A recursive call that goes n levels deep uses O(n) stack space.

internals.title: Where Java puts things
internals.body: Local primitives and references live in the current stack frame. Arrays and objects created with new live on the heap and are freed by the garbage collector once nothing references them. int[] numbers = new int[5] puts five zero-filled ints on the heap and one reference in the frame.

javaExamples.title: Counting loop iterations
javaExamples.explanation: The single loop runs n times; the nested loops run n × n times. Printing the counters shows the growth that Big-O describes.

javaExamples.title: References share one array
javaExamples.explanation: copy and original point at the same heap array, so a write through one is visible through the other. clone() makes a real copy.

complexity.operation: Read or write one array slot
Two nested loops over n items

mistakes: Counting seconds from one run instead of counting steps against n.
Keeping constants: O(2n) and O(n + 10) are both O(n).
Forgetting the extra array you created when stating space complexity.
Assuming int[] b = a copies the array; it copies the reference.
edgeCases: n = 0 and n = 1: loops that never run still count as O(1) work.
int overflow: n × n above about 46,340 does not fit in an int.

assignments.title: Step table
assignments.brief: Write a Java program that prints the step counts for O(n), O(n log n) and O(n²) loops for n = 10, 100 and 1,000, then explain the table in three sentences.

assignments.title: Spot the complexity
assignments.brief: For five short methods your instructor gives you, write the time and space complexity with a one-line reason each.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the time complexity of a loop that doubles i each iteration up to n?
interviewQuestions.answer: O(log n): i takes the values 1, 2, 4, … so the loop runs about log₂n times.

interviewQuestions.question: Why do we drop constants in Big-O?
interviewQuestions.answer: Big-O describes growth as n becomes large; a constant factor does not change the shape of that growth.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the space complexity of a recursive factorial?
interviewQuestions.answer: O(n): each call adds a stack frame and n calls are on the stack at the deepest point.

interviewQuestions.question: Primitive vs reference: what does == compare?
interviewQuestions.answer: For primitives, the values. For references, whether both point at the same object — use equals() to compare contents.

modules.title: Arrays
modules.summary: Fixed-size, contiguous storage with O(1) access by index — the base of most other structures.
modules.overview: An array stores elements of one type in consecutive memory slots, so the address of element i is calculated directly. That makes reading and writing by index O(1), and inserting or removing in the middle O(n) because everything after it has to move. Most interview problems on arrays are about choosing a traversal that avoids that O(n) shifting.
objectives: Declare, fill and traverse one- and two-dimensional arrays in Java.
Explain why index access is O(1) and middle insertion is O(n).
Write a single-pass algorithm that tracks a running value (max, sum, count).
Build a prefix-sum array and use it to answer range sums in O(1).

concepts.title: Indexing and bounds
concepts.body: Valid indexes run from 0 to length − 1. Reading arr[arr.length] throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException. arr.length is a field, not a method.

concepts.title: Single-pass traversal
concepts.body: Many problems need only one pass: keep a running answer (the largest so far, the total so far) and update it as you visit each element. One pass is O(n) time and O(1) space.

concepts.title: Shifting
concepts.body: To insert at index k you must move every element from k to the end one place right. To delete, move them one place left. Both are O(n) in the worst case.

concepts.title: Prefix sums
concepts.body: prefix[i] stores the sum of arr[0..i−1]. The sum of any range arr[l..r] is then prefix[r + 1] − prefix[l], answered in O(1) after O(n) preparation.

internals.title: Contiguous memory
internals.body: For an int[], element i lives at base address + i × 4 bytes. The JVM computes that address in one step, which is why access does not depend on the array size. Java arrays also store their length and are zero-initialised when created with new.

internals.title: 2D arrays are arrays of arrays
internals.body: int[][] grid = new int[3][4] is an array of 3 references, each pointing to its own int[4]. Rows can even have different lengths (jagged arrays).

javaExamples.title: Running maximum and sum in one pass
javaExamples.explanation: One loop updates both answers. Starting max at numbers[0] avoids a wrong answer for all-negative input.

javaExamples.title: Insert at an index by shifting
javaExamples.explanation: Elements from the end down to the insert position move one slot right, then the new value drops into the gap.

javaExamples.title: Prefix sums for range queries
javaExamples.explanation: After one O(n) pass, every range sum is a single subtraction.

complexity.operation: Insert / delete at end (with spare capacity)

complexity.note: Then each range sum is O(1)

mistakes: Looping with i <= arr.length instead of i < arr.length.
Starting a maximum at 0, which is wrong when every value is negative.
Modifying an array while iterating it with an enhanced for loop and expecting indexes.
Forgetting that Arrays.sort changes the original array.
edgeCases: Empty array: decide what to return before indexing numbers[0].

assignments.title: Rotate in place
assignments.brief: Rotate an int array right by k positions using O(1) extra space (hint: three reversals). Print the array after each reversal.

assignments.title: Range-sum service
assignments.brief: Read an array and q queries (l, r). Answer every query with a prefix-sum array and compare the run time with a naive loop for 100,000 queries.

interviewQuestions.question: Why is array access O(1)?
interviewQuestions.answer: The address of element i is base + i × element size, computed in one step, regardless of length.

interviewQuestions.question: Array vs ArrayList?
interviewQuestions.answer: An array has fixed size and can hold primitives. ArrayList grows automatically (amortised O(1) add at the end) and holds objects, so ints are boxed.

interviewQuestions.question: How do you find the second largest element in one pass?
interviewQuestions.answer: Track largest and secondLargest; when a value beats largest, the old largest becomes secondLargest.

interviewQuestions.question: What does a prefix-sum array trade?
interviewQuestions.answer: O(n) extra space and O(n) preparation for O(1) range-sum queries.

modules.title: Strings
modules.summary: Immutable character sequences, StringBuilder, and the character-counting patterns behind most string problems.
modules.overview: A Java String is an immutable sequence of chars. Every "change" — concatenation, replace, toUpperCase — creates a new String. That is safe but can be slow inside loops, which is why StringBuilder exists. Most string problems reduce to array techniques on the characters: two pointers from both ends, or a frequency count of each character.
objectives: Explain String immutability and when to use StringBuilder.
Compare strings correctly with equals() and compareTo().
Use a 26-slot count array to solve anagram and frequency problems in O(n).
Apply two pointers to reverse and palindrome problems.

concepts.title: Immutability
concepts.body: A String object never changes. s = s + "x" builds a new String and points s at it. Inside a loop of n iterations that is O(n²) work in total, because each new string copies the old one.

concepts.title: StringBuilder
concepts.body: StringBuilder keeps a growable char buffer. append is amortised O(1), so building a string of n characters is O(n). Call toString() once at the end.

concepts.title: Equality
concepts.body: == checks whether two references point at the same object. equals() compares characters. Always use equals() for content, and equalsIgnoreCase() when case should not matter.

concepts.title: Character counting
concepts.body: For lowercase letters, int[] count = new int[26] and count[c - 'a']++ records how often each letter appears. Two strings are anagrams exactly when their count arrays are equal.

internals.title: The string pool
internals.body: String literals are stored once in the string pool, so two identical literals may share one object — which is why == sometimes appears to work and then fails for strings built at run time. Never rely on it.

javaExamples.title: Build a string efficiently
javaExamples.explanation: StringBuilder avoids creating a new String on every iteration.

javaExamples.title: Anagram check with a count array
javaExamples.explanation: One pass adds counts for the first word and subtracts for the second; any non-zero slot means they differ.

complexity.operation: Concatenate with + in a loop of n

mistakes: Comparing strings with == instead of equals().
Concatenating inside a loop instead of using StringBuilder.
Using a 26-slot array when the input can contain uppercase letters, digits or spaces.
Forgetting that substring(begin, end) excludes end.
edgeCases: Spaces and punctuation in palindrome checks.

assignments.title: Word frequency
assignments.brief: Read a sentence, split it into words, and print each word with its count, most frequent first.

assignments.title: Compress a string
assignments.brief: Turn "aaabccdddd" into "a3b1c2d4" with a single pass and a StringBuilder. Return the original when the result is not shorter.

interviewQuestions.question: Why are Java Strings immutable?
interviewQuestions.answer: Safety and sharing: strings can be cached in the pool, used as HashMap keys and shared across threads without copying.

interviewQuestions.question: StringBuilder vs StringBuffer?
interviewQuestions.answer: Same API; StringBuffer is synchronized and therefore slower. Use StringBuilder unless several threads share it.

interviewQuestions.question: How do you check if two strings are rotations of each other?
interviewQuestions.answer: They have equal length and the second is a substring of first + first.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the time complexity of checking a palindrome?
interviewQuestions.answer: O(n) time, O(1) space with two pointers from both ends.

modules.title: Searching Algorithms
modules.summary: Linear search for any array, binary search for sorted ones — and binary search on the answer.
modules.overview: Searching asks where a value is, or whether it exists. Without any order, you must check every element: O(n). When the data is sorted, binary search halves the remaining range at every step: O(log n). The same halving idea also solves problems where you search for the smallest answer that satisfies a condition.
objectives: Implement linear search and return the index or −1.
Implement iterative binary search without off-by-one errors.
Find the first and last position of a value with modified binary search.
Recognise "binary search on the answer" problems.

concepts.title: Linear search
concepts.body: Check each element in order until the target is found. Works on any array, sorted or not. Best case O(1), worst case O(n).

concepts.title: Binary search
concepts.body: Keep low and high bounds of where the target could be. Compare with the middle element: if equal, done; if the middle is smaller, the target is to the right; otherwise to the left. Each step discards half.

concepts.title: Safe midpoint
concepts.body: mid = low + (high − low) / 2 avoids the int overflow that (low + high) / 2 can cause when both are near Integer.MAX_VALUE.

concepts.title: Boundaries
concepts.body: To find the first occurrence, keep searching left after a match (high = mid − 1) and remember the match. To find the last, keep searching right.

internals.title: Why log n
internals.body: After k steps the range has n / 2ᵏ elements. The search ends when that reaches 1, so k = log₂n. A million sorted items need at most 20 comparisons.

javaExamples.title: Iterative binary search
javaExamples.explanation: The loop runs while the range [low, high] is not empty. Returns the index or −1.

javaExamples.title: First occurrence of a repeated value
javaExamples.explanation: On a match, record it and keep looking left for an earlier one.

mistakes: Using binary search on unsorted data.
while (low < high) with high = mid − 1, which skips the last candidate.
Setting low = mid instead of mid + 1, causing an infinite loop.
Computing (low + high) / 2 with values near Integer.MAX_VALUE.
edgeCases: Target smaller than every element or larger than every element.
Duplicates when the first or last index is required.

assignments.title: Search insert position
assignments.brief: Return the index where a target is, or where it would be inserted to keep the array sorted. Test with targets below, inside and above the array.

assignments.title: Square root by binary search
assignments.brief: Return the integer square root of n without Math.sqrt by binary searching on the answer between 0 and n.

interviewQuestions.question: When can you not use binary search?
interviewQuestions.answer: When the data has no order (or monotonic condition) that tells you which half to discard.

interviewQuestions.question: What is binary search on the answer?
interviewQuestions.answer: Searching a range of possible answers for the smallest one that satisfies a check that is false then true, like the minimum capacity to ship packages in d days.

interviewQuestions.question: How many comparisons for 1,000,000 sorted elements?
interviewQuestions.answer: At most about 20, because 2²⁰ ≈ 1,048,576.

modules.title: Sorting Algorithms
modules.summary: The O(n²) sorts you can trace by hand, the O(n log n) sorts Java actually uses, and what stability means.
modules.overview: Sorting puts elements in order so that searching, de-duplicating and pairing become easy. The simple sorts — bubble, selection, insertion — are O(n²) and teach how comparisons and swaps add up. Merge sort and quicksort reach O(n log n) by dividing the problem. In real Java code you call Arrays.sort or Collections.sort, and you need to know what they guarantee.
objectives: Trace bubble, selection and insertion sort step by step.
Explain merge sort and why it is O(n log n).
Define stability and say which sorts are stable.
Sort objects with Comparable and Comparator.

concepts.title: Bubble sort
concepts.body: Repeatedly compare neighbours and swap them when out of order. After pass k, the k largest values are in their final places at the end.

concepts.title: Selection sort
concepts.body: For each position, find the smallest remaining value and swap it in. Always n(n−1)/2 comparisons but at most n − 1 swaps.

concepts.title: Insertion sort
concepts.body: Grow a sorted prefix: take the next value and shift larger values right until its place is found. Fast on nearly sorted data and used inside real library sorts for small ranges.

concepts.title: Merge sort
concepts.body: Split the array in half, sort each half recursively, then merge the two sorted halves in O(n). log n levels × O(n) per level = O(n log n). Needs O(n) extra space.

concepts.title: Stability
concepts.body: A sort is stable when equal elements keep their original order. It matters when sorting records by one field after another. Insertion and merge sort are stable; selection sort and typical quicksort are not.

internals.title: What Java uses
internals.body: Arrays.sort on primitives uses a dual-pivot quicksort (fast, not stable, O(n log n) on average). Arrays.sort on objects and Collections.sort use TimSort — a merge/insertion hybrid that is stable and very fast on partly sorted data.

javaExamples.title: Merge sort
javaExamples.explanation: mergeSort splits until single elements remain; merge combines two sorted ranges using a temporary array.

javaExamples.title: Sorting objects with a Comparator
javaExamples.explanation: Sort students by marks (highest first), then by name. List.sort uses TimSort, so it is stable.

complexity.time: O(n log n) average, O(n²) worst

mistakes: Inner loop of bubble sort running to n − 1 every pass instead of n − 1 − i.
Using < instead of <= in merge, which breaks stability.
Writing a Comparator with subtraction (a − b), which can overflow.
Assuming Arrays.sort on int[] is stable — stability is meaningless for primitives but matters for objects.

assignments.title: Count the work
assignments.brief: Instrument bubble, selection and insertion sort to count comparisons and swaps. Run them on sorted, reversed and random arrays of size 1,000 and explain the results.

assignments.title: Leaderboard
assignments.brief: Sort a list of players by score descending, then by time ascending, then by name, using one Comparator chain.

interviewQuestions.question: Which sort would you choose for nearly sorted data?
interviewQuestions.answer: Insertion sort (or TimSort, which exploits existing runs): close to O(n).

interviewQuestions.question: Why is merge sort O(n log n)?
interviewQuestions.answer: There are log n levels of splitting and each level does O(n) merging work.

interviewQuestions.question: What makes quicksort O(n²) in the worst case?
interviewQuestions.answer: Consistently bad pivots, such as always the first element on already sorted data, giving partitions of size n − 1 and 0.

interviewQuestions.question: What is a stable sort and why does it matter?
interviewQuestions.answer: Equal keys keep their input order. It allows multi-key sorting by sorting on the secondary key first, then the primary.

modules.title: Two Pointers and Sliding Window
modules.summary: Move two indexes through an array to replace nested loops with a single pass.

modules.title: Hashing
modules.summary: HashMap and HashSet: average O(1) lookup, counting and de-duplication.

modules.title: Linked Lists
modules.summary: Nodes joined by references: O(1) insertion at a known position, O(n) access by index.
modules.overview: A linked list stores each element in its own node object, and every node holds a reference to the next one. Nothing is contiguous, so there is no index arithmetic: reaching the k-th element means walking k links. In exchange, inserting or removing a node once you are standing next to it is O(1) — only references change, nothing shifts. Linked lists are also the best practice in Java for thinking clearly about references.
objectives: Write a Node class and build a singly linked list by hand.
Insert at the head, insert at the tail and delete by value.
Reverse a linked list iteratively by re-pointing next references.
Use slow and fast pointers to find the middle and detect a cycle.

concepts.title: Nodes and head
concepts.body: Each node has a value and a next reference. The list is known only through head, the reference to the first node. The last node's next is null.

concepts.title: Traversal
concepts.body: Start with current = head and repeat current = current.next until current is null. Every operation that needs a position starts with this walk, which is why access by index is O(n).

concepts.title: Insertion and deletion
concepts.body: To insert after node p: newNode.next = p.next; p.next = newNode. To delete the node after p: p.next = p.next.next. Order matters — re-point the new node before breaking the old link.

concepts.title: Dummy head
concepts.body: A dummy node placed before the real head removes the special case of inserting or deleting at the front. Return dummy.next at the end.

concepts.title: Slow and fast pointers
concepts.body: Move slow one step and fast two steps. When fast reaches the end, slow is at the middle. If the list has a cycle, fast eventually meets slow inside it.

internals.title: Memory layout
internals.body: Each node is a separate object on the heap, typically 16–24 bytes of object header and fields plus the value. Nodes can be anywhere in memory, so walking a list jumps around and is slower in practice than scanning an array, even when both are O(n).

internals.title: java.util.LinkedList
internals.body: Java's LinkedList is doubly linked (each node has next and prev) and keeps references to both head and tail, so adding or removing at either end is O(1). get(i) still walks from the nearer end: O(n).

javaExamples.title: A singly linked list from scratch
javaExamples.explanation: addFirst and addLast build the list; remove deletes the first node with a given value; print walks the links.

javaExamples.title: Reverse a linked list
javaExamples.explanation: Walk once, turning each next reference around. previous ends up as the new head.

javaExamples.title: Middle node with slow and fast pointers
javaExamples.explanation: fast moves twice as fast, so when it runs out slow is halfway.

mistakes: Losing the rest of the list by overwriting current.next before saving it.
Forgetting the empty-list case: head == null.
Not updating head when the first node is deleted (a dummy node avoids this).
Checking fast.next.next without first checking fast.next != null.
edgeCases: Deleting the head or the tail.
Lists with a cycle when a method assumes the end is reachable.

assignments.title: Build your own LinkedList
assignments.brief: Implement addFirst, addLast, removeFirst, removeLast, get(index), size() and reverse() on a singly linked list with a tail reference. Write a main method that tests every method, including the empty list.

assignments.title: Merge two sorted lists
assignments.brief: Given two sorted linked lists, return one sorted list by re-linking the existing nodes (no new nodes except a dummy head).

interviewQuestions.question: Array vs linked list: when would you choose a linked list?
interviewQuestions.answer: When you insert and remove at known positions far more often than you access by index, and you do not need cache-friendly scanning.

interviewQuestions.question: How do you detect a cycle in O(1) space?
interviewQuestions.answer: Floyd's algorithm: slow moves one step, fast two; if they ever meet, there is a cycle.

interviewQuestions.question: How do you find the k-th node from the end in one pass?
interviewQuestions.answer: Move a lead pointer k steps ahead, then move both pointers together until the lead reaches null.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the time complexity of LinkedList.get(i) in Java?
interviewQuestions.answer: O(n): it walks from whichever end is nearer.
